title: Pointed tensor localization comparison with ordinary henselization
statement: Let $A\to B$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ be a prime with inverse image $\mathfrak p\subset A$, and let $R$ and $H$ be ordinary henselizations of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ and $B_{\mathfrak q}$, respectively [def-weil-pbc-henselization-at-prime]. Their structural residue maps give canonical isomorphisms $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\cong R/\mathfrak m_R$ and $\kappa(\mathfrak q)\cong H/\mathfrak m_H$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Put $C=R\otimes_A B$, let $\epsilon:C\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ send $r\otimes b$ to $\overline r\,\overline b$ using $R\to\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, and put $\mathfrak n=\ker\epsilon$ and $D=C_{\mathfrak n}$. Then $\mathfrak n$ is prime, its contractions to $R$ and $B$ are $\mathfrak m_R$ and $\mathfrak q$, and $D$ has residue field canonically $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. Both $B\to D$ and $B\to H$ are ind-etale [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. If $D$ is henselian [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], there is a unique local $B$-algebra isomorphism $e:D\xrightarrow{\sim}H$ inducing the identity of $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. This isomorphism is compatible with the canonical local map $h:R\to H$ obtained from the henselization universal property: $e(r\otimes1)=h(r)$ after localization. Finally, put $T=R\otimes_{A_{\mathfrak p}}B_{\mathfrak q}$ and let $\mathfrak n_T$ be the kernel of its analogous residue evaluation. The maps of the two tensor factors induce a canonical isomorphism $D\cong T_{\mathfrak n_T}$; when $D$ is henselian, its composite with $e^{-1}$ identifies $H$ with $T_{\mathfrak n_T}$ compatibly with $R$ and $B_{\mathfrak q}$. No finite-type or quasi-finiteness hypothesis is imposed on $A\to B$.

proof.text: First recover the structural residue identifications from the universal-property convention for henselization. For either local ring $L=A_{\mathfrak p}$ or $L=B_{\mathfrak q}$, put $k=L/\mathfrak m_L$ and let $L\to J$ be its given henselization. The field $k$ is henselian: its maximal ideal is zero, so the idempotent-lifting condition is the identity condition on every finite $k$-algebra. The universal property supplies a local map $v:J\to k$ extending the quotient of $L$. On residue fields the structural map $i:k\to J/\mathfrak m_J$ and the map $\bar v:J/\mathfrak m_J\to k$ satisfy $\bar v i=1$. Both are field homomorphisms. For $x\in J/\mathfrak m_J$, injectivity of $\bar v$ gives $x=i(\bar v(x))$. Thus $i$ is an isomorphism whose inverse is $\bar v$. Applied to $R$ and $H$ this gives precisely the claimed structural identifications.

source.place: Tags 04GN (lemma-henselization), (4), and 04GQ (definition-henselization); explicit deduction from the initial local-map convention

proof.text: The map $A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ sends $a/s$ to $f(a)/f(s)$; the denominator is invertible because $s\notin\mathfrak p=f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. Its maximal-ideal preimage is $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, so it is local, as is its composite into $H$. The universal property of $R$ now gives the unique local map $h:R\to H$ extending this composite. Its residue map, through step 1, is the structural inclusion $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$: the two maps agree on every fraction from $A_{\mathfrak p}$.

source.place: Tag 04GS (lemma-henselian-functorial), construction of the local map on ordinary henselizations

proof.text: The factor residue maps agree on $A$, so the tensor-product relations give the ring map $\epsilon(r\otimes b)=\bar r\bar b$. Its kernel $\mathfrak n$ is prime since its target is a field and $\epsilon(1)=1$. The residue maps $R\to\kappa(\mathfrak p)\hookrightarrow\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ and $B\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ have kernels $\mathfrak m_R$ and $\mathfrak q$, respectively, giving both contractions. Extend evaluation to $\epsilon_D:D\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ by $c/s\mapsto\epsilon(c)/\epsilon(s)$. Its kernel is $\mathfrak nD$, the maximal ideal of $D$. It is onto: any element of $\kappa(\mathfrak q)=B_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}$ is represented by $b/t$ with $t\notin\mathfrak q$, and is the image of $(1\otimes b)/(1\otimes t)$. Hence $D/\mathfrak nD\cong\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. In particular the induced map $B_{\mathfrak q}\to D$ is local and induces the identity on this residue field.

source.place: Tag 05WP (lemma-quasi-finite-henselization), pointed localization in the proof; Tag 00CO (definition-localization), fraction verification

proof.text: Apply the existing prime-henselization ind-etaleness lemma to $(A,\mathfrak p,R)$ and $(B,\mathfrak q,H)$. It gives ind-etaleness of the specified maps $A\to R$ and $B\to H$, with no finiteness hypothesis. Base change of $A\to R$ along $A\to B$, using stability of ind-etale maps, gives ind-etaleness of $B\to C=R\otimes_A B$ (interchanging tensor factors by $r\otimes b\mapsto b\otimes r$).

source.place: Tag 04GN (lemma-henselization), (2); Tag 097J (lemma-base-change-ind-etale), base change of the specified structural map

proof.text: To pass from $C$ to $D$, use the small directed set of finite subsets $F\subset C\setminus\mathfrak n$, with term $C_{s_F}$ where $s_F=\prod_{s\in F}s$. The set is nonempty and directed by union. For $F\subset G$, write $s_G=s_Fs_{G\setminus F}$; invertibility of $s_G$ makes $s_F$ invertible, giving the unique structural localization map, and uniqueness makes these maps compose. This diagram has colimit $C_{\mathfrak n}$ as $C$-algebras: a compatible family into a $C$-algebra $E$ amounts exactly to its structural map making each $s\notin\mathfrak n$ invertible, with fraction formula $c/s\mapsto c\,s^{-1}$. The empty subset gives the term $C$, so these maps and their unique fraction extensions preserve the specified $C$-algebra structures. Each $C\to C_{s_F}$ is etale and finitely presented by the existing etale-localization lemma, applied to the identity $C$-algebra. Thus this is an ind-etale presentation of $C\to D$. Composing with the ind-etale map $B\to C$ of step 4 proves that $B\to D$ is ind-etale.

source.place: Tag 05WP (lemma-quasi-finite-henselization), proof sentence about localization as a filtered etale colimit; Tag 00U2 (lemma-etale), (1), and Tag 097K (lemma-composition-ind-etale)

proof.text: Now assume $D$ is henselian. Apply the prescribed-residue lifting lemma over the base ring $B$, with source algebra $D$, source prime $\mathfrak nD$, target $H$, and residue map $\mathrm{id}_{\kappa(\mathfrak q)}$. Steps 3--5 verify all its hypotheses: the source is ind-etale over $B$, both maximal ideals contract to $\mathfrak q$, the target is henselian, and both residue fields have the specified identification. Under those structural identifications the residue maps from $B$ agree with $B\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, so the prescribed identity is a map of $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$-algebras, as the lifting lemma requires. It gives a unique local $B$-algebra map $e:D\to H$ with that residue map. Apply the same lemma with source $H$ and target $D$ to obtain $j:H\to D$. Both composites are local $B$-algebra maps inducing the identity on the relevant residue field. Apply uniqueness once to source and target $D$, and once to source and target $H$, comparing with the identity maps. It follows that $je=1_D$ and $ej=1_H$. Thus $e$ is the asserted unique local residue-compatible $B$-algebra isomorphism.

source.place: Tags 08HR (lemma-map-into-henselian-colimit) and 08HT (lemma-uniqueness-henselian), inverse-composite argument in the proof of Tag 05WP

proof.text: The canonical map $a:R\to D$, $r\mapsto(r\otimes1)/1$, is local by the contraction computed in step 3. Consequently $ea$ and $h$ are local maps $R\to H$. They agree on $A_{\mathfrak p}$ because $e$ is a $B$-algebra map, and agreement on $A$ extends to its inverted denominators. The uniqueness clause in the universal property of $R$ therefore gives $ea=h$, which is the required compatibility on every $r$.

source.place: Tag 04GS (lemma-henselian-functorial); the factor compatibility in Tag 05WP (lemma-quasi-finite-henselization)

proof.text:
For the final comparison, define $\epsilon_T:T	o\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ by $r\otimes(b/t)\mapsto ar r ar b/ ar t$. It is balanced over $A_{\mathfrak p}$; its kernel $\mathfrak n_T$ is prime. The map $u:C	o T$ sends $r\otimes b$ to $r\otimes(b/1)$ and satisfies $\epsilon_Tu=\epsilon$. Hence each $s
otin\mathfrak n$ becomes a unit in $T_{\mathfrak n_T}$, giving $\alpha:D	o T_{\mathfrak n_T}$ with $\alpha(c/s)=u(c)/u(s)$. Conversely, in $D$ every $1\otimes t$ for $t
otin\mathfrak q$ is invertible. Define $v:T	o D$ by $v(r\otimes(b/t))=((r\otimes b)/1)((1\otimes t)/1)^{-1}$. This is balanced over $A_{\mathfrak p}$ since the two structural maps agree on $A$ and on inverses of $A\setminus\mathfrak p$. Its reduction is $\epsilon_T$. If $z
otin\mathfrak n_T$, then $v(z)$ has nonzero residue, so it is a unit in the local ring $D$. Thus $v$ extends to $ eta:T_{\mathfrak n_T}	o D$ by $z/w\mapsto v(z)v(w)^{-1}$. The composite $ eta\alpha$ fixes $C$ and all its inverted denominators, hence is $1_D$. The composite $\alpha eta$ fixes $R$, $B_{\mathfrak q}$ and inverses of elements outside $\mathfrak n_T$, hence fixes every tensor and every fraction, so is the identity. This proves the canonical factor-compatible isomorphism. When $D$ is henselian, $\alpha e^{-1}:H	o T_{\mathfrak n_T}$ is compatible with $R$ by step 7 and with $B_{\mathfrak q}$ since it agrees on $B$ and inverses of $B\setminus\mathfrak q$.
